sentences.t: The headquarters of the world's largest oil company told its staff not to come in.

Saudi Aramco evacuated its Dhahran campus and moved employees to remote work after a series of attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement - the first such evacuation since the Iran war began in February (Reuters, reported by CNBC and The National).

The attacks had turned lethal two days earlier: a drone aimed at the Shaybah oilfield in the Eastern Province killed two people and injured two, and a strike on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam killed at least two and injured eight, according to Saudi state media.
Over 48 hours the Houthis also claimed the Defence Ministry in Riyadh, an Aramco site in Yanbu and Abha airport.
The US State Department ordered non-essential personnel out of the kingdom.
The market's answer came in two prints.
In the Gulf evening, Brent traded at $117.20.
By the New York close, Brent futures had settled at $116.72, up 3.1% on the day and 6.2% on the week; US WTI settled at $103.27.
And yet, inside the same day's reporting, sat the fact this whole essay hangs on.

"Production and export flows through the Strait of Hormuz are still holding at close to pre-conflict levels, though at elevated shipping rates," said Edward Bell, head of research at MUFG, and Soojin Kim, research analyst at the group, to The National.
The oil is flowing.
The price is rising anyway.
That difference has a name, a history and a cost - and India pays the bill.
Eight months ago, on 28 February, Israel and the United States attacked Iran, killing Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and other senior officials.

Iran answered with strikes on Israel and across the Gulf, and asserted control over the Strait of Hormuz - the channel for about a fifth of the world's oil consumption (Reuters's Hormuz explainer; the US Energy Information Administration calls it the world's most important oil chokepoint).
On 8 March, Iran named one of Khamenei's sons, Mojtaba, as the new supreme leader; he has not been seen in public since and is believed to have been hurt in the opening strikes.
A two-week ceasefire followed on 7 April - Israel not included - and on 21 April, President Trump extended it indefinitely.
It broke on 7 June, when Iran fired on Israel for the first time since April.
A week later Trump announced an interim deal; it was signed around 26-27 June, starting a 60-day clock toward a permanent end to the war.

By 12 July the deal was already fraying - strikes traded both ways, Trump threatening Iran's civilian infrastructure and musing about seizing Kharg Island, the terminal for most of Iran's crude exports.
(All from AP's running timeline of the war, updated 12 July.)
October brought the next turn.
On Monday, Brent had slipped from $110 as traders priced in more Russian supply - the war premium bleeding out, as it does.
Then came Wednesday: Shaybah, Dammam, the claims on Riyadh and Yanbu, the Dhahran evacuation, the State Department pullout.

Trump said Wednesday the US is "not negotiating" with Iran and something would happen "fairly soon"; US officials told the New York Times that plans exist for fresh strikes after the midterm elections.
Iran's army chief told the Tasnim agency his forces are ready for "asymmetric warfare".
Traders, CNBC reports, now expect US strikes to resume in the coming weeks.
A Libyan supply disruption - real, but small - tightened the physical market just enough to give the fear somewhere to sit.
A shortage is a physical fact: there is less oil than buyers want, and the price rises until someone goes without.
A premium is a probability: there is exactly enough oil today, but a chance there will not be tomorrow, and every refiner pays a little extra to be sure of having it.
Shortages are slow to form and slow to fix.
Premiums form in an afternoon and vanish over a weekend.
This week is a premium.
The flows through Hormuz are near pre-conflict levels (MUFG's read on Friday).
Nobody's refinery has gone short.
What changed is the perceived odds of a US strike on Iran and a Saudi-Houthi war sliding back into something wider - and crude repriced those odds by about $6.7 a barrel in five sessions.

That is not a comforting fact, but it is a useful one, because premiums behave in ways shortages do not: they spike on headlines, they decay on quiet days, and they unwind completely if the feared event does not arrive.

And the premium has come off before: by this Monday, with Russian supply prospects improving, the five-month rally was being openly questioned - Brent slipped back from $110 before Wednesday's attacks repriced it.
The premium is real money while it lasts - it just does not last by itself.
The $116.72 print is not what oil costs.
It is what the fear of a strike costs, added to what oil costs - and the two parts have very different shelf lives.
India imports 88.6% of the crude it consumes (April to January of FY26, on Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell data via the Indian Express).
That dependence gives the arithmetic its blunt edge: every $1 on the barrel price adds up to $2 billion a year to the import bill (the Indian Express's explainer on the PPAC data).
Now the week's transaction, explicitly.
Brent went from about $110 on Monday to $116.72 on Friday - call it $6.7.

At the PPAC ratio, that is up to about $13.4 billion a year of extra import cost if it holds - an illustrative sensitivity, holding the import basket and the exchange rate constant, not a measure of what this week has already cost.
At Friday's rupee (94.93 per dollar), it is roughly ₹1.27 lakh crore.
The Jio Platforms IPO that closed the same day - the largest in Indian history - raised ₹30,213 crore.
The week's oil move, on that same illustrative annualisation, is about four Jio IPOs.
That is the size of the premium, stated in the week's own units.
The channels from that number to an Indian household are already visible.
The rupee fell 12 paise to a provisional 94.93 on Friday, a second straight down day, with traders citing crude (PTI).

HPCL's results on Thursday showed what the squeeze does to a refiner-marketer: profit down 9% year on year to ₹3,483 crore as higher crude prices and tax expenses squeezed marketing margins, even with product sales up 26% (Business Standard, Moneycontrol).

BPCL's filing on Friday put the cumulative LPG under-recovery buffer at ₹17,334.40 crore - the shortfall the company has absorbed selling cooking gas below cost, with ₹3,796.98 crore of government compensation recognised in the half.
At $116, the resolution runs through some mix of retail price changes, government compensation and refiner margins - the filing sizes the buffer; it does not say who pays.
The first bill lands on the import ledger.
The second lands on the cost of money, and it may be the larger one.
Oil is the fastest-moving ingredient in inflation, and inflation is what central banks answer to.

On Friday, CME's FedWatch tool - the market's own pricing - showed traders putting a 92% chance on the Federal Reserve holding rates at its 27-28 October meeting, but a 78% probability of a December rate HIKE (cited by CNBC).
A hike: not a hold, not the cut that was the base case weeks ago.
Last week's US consumer and producer inflation came in hot, and Friday's flash PMI showed selling prices at their highest since 2022 even as activity cooled (composite 57.6 against 58.4).
The Personal Consumption Expenditures report on 29 October is the next hard number.
Watch what this did to gold, because it is the cleanest proof of the mechanism.

Gold is the ancient war hedge - and it just had its worst week since June, down 4%, with spot trading at $3,998.49 on Friday afternoon (2:27 PM EDT) - under $4,000 for the first time since mid-July - while December futures settled at $4,007.90.

Missiles flew and gold fell, because the missiles' effect on interest rates mattered more than the missiles: higher-for-longer yields make a zero-yield metal expensive to hold, and Thursday's AI selloff forced funds to sell whatever was sellable to meet margin calls (analyst Jim Wyckoff's account to CNBC).
The same repricing reached Mumbai: midcaps fell 2.2% on a day the Sensex fell 0.2%, because long-duration assets discount at the new rate path first.
India's 10-year government bond yield closed Friday at 7.47% - a tenth straight weekly rise, the longest losing streak for Indian government bonds in 30 years (Business Standard).
Three things would turn this premium into a shortage, and they are all watchable.

First, a strike that hits Gulf production or loading infrastructure rather than symbols - the Shaybah drone killed people but did not stop a barrel; a hit that does stop barrels is a different market.

Second, the Strait itself: Iran still insists it alone controls Hormuz, and thousands of mariners were waiting out the war's terms there as of July; any boarding, mining or insurance withdrawal is the physical threshold.
Third, a strike-after-the-midterms scenario playing out in public, because it converts a headline risk into a dated calendar risk.
The invalidation runs the other way too.

If the weekend passes quietly, if the interim-deal track revives - it survived one unravelling already - or if Russian and Saudi barrels visibly cover the gap (Monday's slip from $110 came on exactly that prospect), the premium unwinds as fast as it built, and the India math above shrinks with it.
The honest position for a Saturday morning: the flows say calm, the evacuations say otherwise, and the price is the argument between them.
The week hands the decision to a single day.

On Wednesday 28 October, in Washington, the Federal Reserve ends its meeting and tells the world whether the December hike is real; in Mumbai, that same morning, Jio Platforms lists at ₹10.3 lakh crore of valuation on the largest bid haul an Indian IPO has ever seen; and on Thursday the PCE report prints the inflation number both will live with.
Oil will vote first - the weekend's headlines set Monday's open - but the premium's fate is decided by whether anything actually explodes between now and then.
India, importing 88.6% of its oil, does not get a vote.
It only gets the bill.
The one number to hold through it: $1 a barrel equals up to $2 billion a year.
When the anchors shout $120 or $100 next week, you can convert it yourself, in the time it takes to read the ticker.
